Zooming In On Success Dragon International Holdings' Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

For the year to March 2026, Success Dragon International Holdings had an accrual ratio of 0.96. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. To wit, the company did not generate one whit of free cashflow in that time. In the last twelve months it actually had negative free cash flow, with an outflow of HK$22m despite its profit of HK$72.9m, mentioned above. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of HK$22m, this year, indicates high risk.

data.title: Becton Dickinson (BDX) Stock Shrugs Off Profit Strength As Tariffs Bite
data.description:
Becton Dickinson stock barely flinched after earnings, slipping just 0.1% to about US$176, even as the company put a very different picture on the tape. The headline is profit power. Adjusted earnings per share came in at US$3.23 and adjusted operating margin held at a solid 24.9% in a quarter that management framed as the first real test for “New BD.”

For a company often treated as a slow and steady medical technology compounder, that kind of earnings print, plus revenue of US$5.0b, sets up a more interesting debate than the flat share price suggests.

Becton Dickinson’s Margin Story Meets Its First Real Test

The bullish story around Becton Dickinson hinges on “New BD” using BD Excellence, modernization and a refreshed portfolio to deliver steadier growth with stronger margins and free cash flow. Q3 results hit several of those milestones. Revenue grew 4.4% on an FX neutral basis with management saying more than 90% of the portfolio delivered high single digit growth. That supports the idea of a broad based engine rather than a few hot products.

The more important claim is structural margin improvement. Here the picture is mixed but still supportive. Adjusted operating margin of 24.9% was slightly lower year on year, yet plants delivered about 8% productivity, record low back orders and service levels above 90%, while tariffs and targeted sales and R&D spend weighed on the reported figure. Free cash flow of US$1.7b year to date, up 45%, and US$2.3b of buybacks show the capital return element of the thesis is firmly on track.

Becton Dickinson Bears See Some Concerns Confirmed

The cautious view on Becton Dickinson argues that utilization risk, price pressure and stubborn costs will cap both growth and margins. This quarter does not fully disprove that. Reported revenue declined 9.6% year on year and adjusted operating margin slipped by roughly 100 to 130 basis points to 24.9%. That points to some pressure on the core profitability story, even with plant productivity running at about 8% and service levels above 90%.

Bears have also warned that inflation and tariffs could blunt BD Excellence benefits. The roughly 110 basis point tariff drag and continued stepped up selling and R&D spend fit that concern. Quality and regulatory worries remain on the radar, given the recent voluntary recall of skin prep applicators, although there is no quantified earnings hit yet. The market’s flat reaction, with the stock down 0.1%, suggests these execution and cost debates are still unresolved.
